<span class="index">01</span>

<span class="kicker">Section 01</span>

# 📘 What This Repository Is

A public, beginner-oriented path to learning AWS CDK (Python) without an AWS account.

---

<span class="kicker">In one paragraph</span>

## 44 modules, 11 phases, one pattern each

`learning-cdk-python` teaches AWS with the
[AWS Cloud Development Kit (CDK) v2](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/v2/guide/home.html)
in Python, managed with [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/). It is **44 small,
independent modules** (`modules/01_iam` → `modules/44_resource_quotas`),
each teaching one AWS service through a minimal, deployable CDK stack plus
a README — grouped into **11 phases**, from identity foundations to
governance and operations.

<div class="stats">
  <div class="stat"><span class="num">44</span><span class="label">modules, one AWS service each</span></div>
  <div class="stat"><span class="num">11</span><span class="label">learning phases</span></div>
  <div class="stat"><span class="num">$0</span><span class="label">cost to complete it, via floci</span></div>
</div>

<span class="kicker">The 11 phases, at a glance</span>

<span class="kicker">Every module follows the same shape</span>

## The module contract (`CLAUDE.md`, section 3)

<div class="cards">
  <div class="card">
    <div class="icon">🧱</div>
    <h4>One `Stack` subclass</h4>
    <p>Fixed <code>__init__(self, scope, construct_id, *, config, **kwargs)</code> signature, plus module-level <code>STACK_ID</code> and <code>STACK_CLASS</code>.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="card">
    <div class="icon">🔍</div>
    <h4>No manual wiring in `app.py`</h4>
    <p><code>pkgutil.iter_modules()</code> discovers every <code>modules/*/stack.py</code> automatically — adding a module never means editing <code>app.py</code>.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="card">
    <div class="icon">🏷️</div>
    <h4>Standard tags + a README</h4>
    <p><code>apply_standard_tags()</code> once, <code>apply_name_tag()</code> per resource, and a README matching <code>modules/03_vpc/README.md</code>'s section structure.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="card">
    <div class="icon">✅</div>
    <h4>A unit test, always</h4>
    <p>One <code>tests/unit/test_NN_service.py</code> per module, asserting on the synthesized CloudFormation template — see <code>docs/TESTING.md</code>.</p>
  </div>
</div>

---

<span class="kicker">The most important rule</span>

## Do not invent things

<div class="columns">
  <div class="col">
    <h4>✅ Every claim is checked</h4>
    <p>Every CDK construct name, property, and AWS behavior claim must come from a source actually consulted — the CDK API Reference, the CDK Developer Guide, or the AWS service's own docs.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="col dark">
    <h4>🚫 No shortcuts</h4>
    <p>Prefer the L2 construct; fall back to the L1 <code>Cfn*</code> construct (documented explicitly) when no L2 exists; never use an <code>-alpha</code> package; never fabricate a construct for a service with no CloudFormation resource (Service Quotas).</p>
  </div>
</div>

> A number or version-specific detail (a default retention period, a current image tag) is the highest-risk content — always re-checked against current docs, never recalled from memory.

---

<span class="kicker">Non-negotiable, every module</span>

## Tagging and naming policy

<div class="cards">
  <div class="card"><h4><code>Name</code></h4><p>e.g. <code>learning-cdk-python-dev-orders-queue</code> — AWS's own console-display tag, applied per resource.</p></div>
  <div class="card"><h4><code>environment</code></h4><p>e.g. <code>dev</code>, <code>staging</code>, <code>prod</code></p></div>
  <div class="card"><h4><code>product</code></h4><p>e.g. <code>learning-cdk-python</code></p></div>
  <div class="card"><h4><code>team-owner</code></h4><p>e.g. <code>platform-engineering</code></p></div>
  <div class="card"><h4><code>pci</code></h4><p><code>true</code>/<code>false</code> — PCI DSS scope</p></div>
  <div class="card"><h4><code>cell-based</code> / <code>cell-id</code></h4><p>whether the resource is part of a cell-based deployment</p></div>
</div>

Applied by [`shared/tagging.py`](../../shared/tagging.py); physical names built by [`shared/naming.py`](../../shared/naming.py) (`-`-separated). No stack hardcodes an AWS account ID, region, or Availability Zone — see `REQUIREMENTS.md` sections 7–9.

# 🧰 The Toolchain

The exact tools this repository runs on, from Python packaging to CDK, testing, and containers.

<div class="logo-row">
  <img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="AWS Cloud Development Kit" />

---

<span class="kicker">Straight from the AWS CDK's own GitHub README</span>

## What the AWS CDK actually is

<div class="logo-row">
  <img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="AWS Cloud Development Kit" style="max-height:70px" />
</div>

<div class="quote">
  "The AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) is an open-source software
  development framework to define cloud infrastructure in code and
  provision it through AWS CloudFormation."
  <cite>— aws/aws-cdk, github.com/aws/aws-cdk</cite>
</div>

That's the whole idea: `modules/03_vpc/stack.py` is Python code; `cdk synth` turns it into a CloudFormation template; CloudFormation (emulated by floci, or real AWS) creates the actual resources.

---

<!-- _class: dense-table -->

<span class="kicker">One table, every tool</span>

## What's used, and what for

| Tool | Role |
|---|---|
| [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) | Python package/venv manager — installs `aws-cdk-lib`, `constructs`, `boto3`, dev tools into `.venv/` |
| [AWS CDK v2 (Python)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/v2/guide/home.html), `aws-cdk-lib==2.271.0` | Describes AWS resources as Python code; synthesizes CloudFormation |
| `constructs`, `boto3` | CDK's construct base library; AWS SDK for Python (used by a few module scripts) |
| [floci](https://floci.io) (Docker) | Free, local AWS emulator — every module deploys here first |
| Docker + Docker Compose v2 | Runs floci and its optional consoles (`docker-compose.yml`) |
| [mise](https://mise.jdx.dev) (optional) | Pins/installs the exact Python, Node.js 26, npm 11, and AWS CLI v2 versions (`mise.toml` / `.python-version`) |
| `pytest`, `mypy`, `ruff` | Unit tests (`aws_cdk.assertions`), type checks, and linting |
| Node.js 26 + npm 11 (via mise) | Runs the AWS CDK Toolkit (`cdk` CLI) and, optionally, Mermaid/Marp CLIs |

---

<span class="kicker">Python packaging</span>

## uv — the package/venv manager

<div class="steps">
  <div class="step"><span class="n">1</span><p><strong>One command, one venv</strong> — <code>uv sync</code> reads <code>pyproject.toml</code>/<code>uv.lock</code> and builds <code>.venv/</code> with the pinned Python (<code>.python-version</code> → 3.12).</p></div>
  <div class="step"><span class="n">2</span><p><strong>Every command runs through it</strong> — <code>uv run cdk ...</code>, <code>uv run pytest</code>, <code>uv run ruff</code>; no manual <code>source .venv/bin/activate</code> needed.</p></div>
  <div class="step"><span class="n">3</span><p><strong>Wired into <code>cdk.json</code></strong> — its <code>"app"</code> entry is literally <code>"uv run python app.py"</code>, so the CDK CLI always uses the right interpreter.</p></div>
</div>

```bash
uv sync                          # installs aws-cdk-lib, constructs, boto3, pytest, mypy, ruff
uv run cdk --version              # confirms the CDK Toolkit is reachable through uv
```

---

<span class="kicker">Python code → CloudFormation</span>

## The AWS CDK v2 workflow

<div class="flow">
  <div class="flow-row">
    <div class="flow-box"><strong>✏️ Edit code</strong><span><code>modules/NN_service/stack.py</code></span></div>
    <div class="flow-arrow">→</div>
    <div class="flow-box"><strong>🧵 app.py wires it up</strong><span>discovers it + shared config/tags/naming</span></div>
    <div class="flow-arrow">→</div>
    <div class="flow-box accent"><strong>🧪 cdk synth</strong><span>CloudFormation template — free, no credentials</span></div>
  </div>
  <div class="flow-arrow down">↓</div>
  <div class="flow-row">
    <div class="flow-box dark"><strong>🚀 cdk deploy</strong><span>floci <code>:4566</code>, or a real AWS account</span></div>
    <div class="flow-arrow">→</div>
    <div class="flow-box"><strong>✅ Resources exist</strong><span>verify: AWS CLI / <code>boto3</code> / floci console</span></div>
    <div class="flow-arrow">→</div>
    <div class="flow-box"><strong>🧹 cdk destroy</strong><span>back to nothing</span></div>
  </div>
</div>

<p class="flow-caption">Full diagram (with the endpoint decision spelled out): <code>docs/images/01-cdk-workflow.svg</code> — see <code>docs/ARCHITECTURE.md</code> section 1</p>

---

<span class="kicker">Reading the diagram</span>

## `synth` is free, `deploy` is the one that talks to an endpoint

<div class="columns">
  <div class="col">
    <h4>🧪 <code>cdk synth</code></h4>
    <p>Only reads your code and <code>shared/config.py</code>/<code>tagging.py</code>/<code>naming.py</code>. Needs no AWS credentials, creates nothing — safe to run constantly while learning.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="col dark">
    <h4>🚀 <code>cdk deploy</code> / <code>cdk destroy</code></h4>
    <p>The only commands that talk to an actual endpoint — <code>http://localhost:4566</code> (floci) when <code>AWS_ENDPOINT_URL</code> is set, or a real AWS account/region otherwise.</p>
  </div>
</div>

```bash
uv run cdk list                                          # every module's stack id
uv run cdk synth VpcStack                                 # safe, local, no endpoint call
uv run cdk deploy VpcStack --require-approval never       # creates resources (floci by default)
uv run cdk destroy VpcStack                                # tears them back down
```

---

<span class="kicker">Quality gates</span>

## Testing, type-checking, and linting

```bash
uv run pytest                            # every unit test — no Docker/floci/AWS credentials needed
uv run pytest tests/unit/test_03_vpc.py -v
make typecheck                           # type checks with mypy (from __future__ import annotations everywhere)
uv run ruff check .                        # linting
make check                                # OS + every required/recommended/optional tool
```

<div class="stats">
  <div class="stat"><span class="num">199</span><span class="label">unit tests, 43 test files — one per module with a stack.py</span></div>

# 🌐 floci — the Local AWS Emulator

What it emulates, how to start it, and how the AWS CLI/SDK/CDK all talk to it.

<div class="logo-row">
  <img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="floci" />
</div>

---

<span class="kicker">Straight from floci's own README (github.com/floci-io/floci)</span>

## floci, in its own words

<div class="logo-row">
  <img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="floci" style="max-height:56px" />
</div>

<div class="quote">
  "Floci is a free, open-source local AWS emulator for development,
  testing, and CI. It gives you AWS-shaped services on your machine
  without requiring a cloud account, an auth token, or paid feature
  gates. Point your AWS SDK, CLI, Terraform, CDK, OpenTofu, or test
  suite at <code>http://localhost:4566</code> and keep your existing
  workflows."
  <cite>— floci-io/floci README</cite>
</div>

<div class="tag-row">
  <span class="pill" style="background:#0B1F3A;">MIT licensed</span>
  <span class="pill">Forever free</span>
  <span class="pill" style="background:#0B1F3A;">Drop-in AWS compatible</span>
</div>

---

<span class="kicker">Official feature list</span>

## Why every module here deploys to floci first

<div class="cards">
  <div class="card"><div class="icon">🏠</div><h4>Local AWS, no cloud account</h4><p>AWS-shaped services on your own machine — no credentials to create, leak, or pay for.</p></div>
  <div class="card"><div class="icon">🐳</div><h4>Real Docker where fidelity matters</h4><p>Some services (Lambda, RDS, ECS, EKS...) run as actual containers, not shallow mocks.</p></div>
  <div class="card"><div class="icon">🔌</div><h4>Drop-in AWS compatibility</h4><p>The AWS CLI, `boto3`, Terraform, and the AWS CDK all "just work" against it.</p></div>
  <div class="card"><div class="icon">⚡</div><h4>Fast enough for CI</h4><p>floci.io's own numbers: a ~24 ms cold start, ~13 MiB idle memory footprint.</p></div>
</div>

<p style="font-size:0.62em;color:#5A6784;margin-top:10px;">Source: <a href="https://floci.io">floci.io</a> and the floci README (github.com/floci-io/floci) — re-check before quoting exact numbers, they're the vendor's own benchmark, not independently verified here.</p>

---

<span class="kicker">Two ways to start it</span>

## Option A: docker compose · Option B: floci-cli

<div class="columns">
  <div class="col">
    <h4>🐳 Option A — this repo's <code>docker-compose.yml</code></h4>
    <pre><code>docker compose up -d floci
export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:4566
export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=test
export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=test
export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1</code></pre>
  </div>
  <div class="col dark">
    <h4>⚡ Option B — <a href="https://github.com/floci-io/floci-cli">floci-cli</a></h4>
    <pre><code>floci start        # launches + waits for readiness
eval $(floci env)  # exports the 4 vars above
floci status        # container state and health
floci stop</code></pre>
  </div>
</div>

Use either option, not both at once — they bind the same port. See [`.env.example`](../../.env.example) for a file you can `source` instead of exporting by hand.

## The built-in floci-ui web console

A browser-based console for inspecting what you just created — S3 buckets,
DynamoDB tables, SQS queues, Lambda logs, and more — ships **inside** the
`floci` container itself (it's the floci-ui project's own UI, embedded):

```
http://localhost:4566/_floci/ui
```

<div class="cards cols-1">
  <div class="card"><h4>Enabled by one env var</h4><p><code>FLOCI_SERVICES_UI_ENABLED: "true"</code>, already set in this repository's <code>docker-compose.yml</code>, plus the Docker socket mounted so the console can run its own sidecar container.</p></div>
</div>

This console is enough for every module in this learning path — floci-dash on the next slides is an optional, alternative console.

## floci-ui — also available as a standalone project

<div class="steps">
  <div class="step"><span class="n">1</span><p><strong>Same UI, a separate deployment</strong> — its own frontend + API project, not the built-in console. No published image: its own compose file <em>builds</em> from source.</p></div>
  <div class="step"><span class="n">2</span><p><strong>Clone it next to this repo</strong> — <code>git clone https://github.com/floci-io/floci-ui.git ../floci-ui</code> (or point <code>FLOCI_UI_REPO_PATH</code> elsewhere).</p></div>
  <div class="step"><span class="n">3</span><p><strong>Start it with a Compose profile</strong> — builds and runs alongside the one <code>floci</code> service, not a second emulator.</p></div>
</div>

```bash
docker compose --profile floci-ui up -d --build
# floci-ui (frontend):  http://localhost:4500
# floci-api (backend):  http://localhost:4501
```

## floci-dash — a second console

<div class="logo-row small">

<div class="quote">
  "AWS Console-style web UI for Floci — the local AWS emulator." Built

## Every console, side by side

```bash
docker compose --profile floci-ui --profile floci-dash up -d --build
```

| Port | Service | Always on? |
|---|---|---|
| `4566` | floci (AWS-compatible API + built-in `/_floci/ui` console) | ✅ yes |
| `4500` | floci-ui (standalone frontend) | only `--profile floci-ui` |
| `4501` | floci-api (standalone backend) | only `--profile floci-ui` |
| `9877` | floci-dash (dashboard) | only `--profile floci-dash` |

Independent Compose profiles, different ports — enable the ones you want, or none at all.

> **Found while preparing this deck:** the `floci/floci` image ships no `curl`/`wget`, so `docker-compose.yml`'s healthcheck (which `floci-dash`'s `depends_on: condition: service_healthy` relies on) now probes the port with bash's own `/dev/tcp` instead — fixed and verified against a real `docker compose --profile floci-dash up -d` run.

# 💻 Running the Practical Lab

From a fresh clone to your first `cdk deploy`, and a worked example.

---

<span class="kicker">Before you start</span>

## Prerequisites

| Tool | What for |
|---|---|
| Python 3.14 (via uv or mise) | runs the CDK app and the unit tests |
| uv | Python package/venv manager |
| Node.js 26 + npm 11 (via mise) | runs the AWS CDK Toolkit (`cdk` CLI) |
| Docker + Docker Compose v2 | runs floci and its optional consoles |
| AWS CLI v2 (via mise), `make`, `git` | manual inspection of floci; orchestration |

Supported: Ubuntu 22.04+ (`amd64`) and macOS 13+ (`arm64`/`amd64`). Windows: use WSL2. Full list: [`REQUIREMENTS.md`](../../REQUIREMENTS.md).

```bash
git clone <this-repository-url> && cd learning-cdk-python
make check                            # confirms everything above is actually installed
```

---

<span class="kicker">Zero to your first deploy</span>

## The 9-step walkthrough (`REQUIREMENTS.md` §0)

<div class="steps">
  <div class="step"><span class="n">1-3</span><p>Install the tools, clone the repo, run <code>make check</code> to confirm your machine is ready.</p></div>
  <div class="step"><span class="n">4</span><p><code>uv sync</code> — installs every Python dependency into <code>.venv/</code>.</p></div>
  <div class="step"><span class="n">5-6</span><p><code>docker compose up -d floci</code>, then point your terminal at it: <code>cp .env.example .env; set -a; source .env; set +a</code>.</p></div>
  <div class="step"><span class="n">7</span><p><code>uv run cdk --version</code> and <code>uv run cdk list</code> — should print every module's stack id, no errors.</p></div>
  <div class="step"><span class="n">8-9</span><p>Follow <code>modules/01_iam/README.md</code>, deploy/destroy it, then <code>docker compose down</code> when done for the day.</p></div>
</div>

---

<span class="kicker">Copy-paste ready</span>

## Deploying and destroying one module

```bash
uv sync
docker compose up -d floci
cp .env.example .env; set -a; source .env; set +a

uv run cdk list                                            # see every module's stack id
uv run cdk synth VpcStack                                   # preview the CloudFormation template
uv run cdk deploy VpcStack --require-approval never          # create the resources, against floci
uv run cdk destroy VpcStack                                   # clean up when you're done
```

Verify what got created through the floci console at
`http://localhost:4566/_floci/ui`, or with the AWS CLI pointed at the same endpoint.

## Worked example: `modules/03_vpc`

`modules/03_vpc` is the module every other one was written to match. Its
`ec2.Vpc(..., max_azs=2, nat_gateways=0, subnet_configuration=[...])` call
creates one VPC, one Internet Gateway, 4 subnets (public + private-isolated
× 2 AZs), and one security group:

<div class="flow">
  <div class="flow-row">
    <div class="flow-box dark" style="max-width:300px;"><strong>Amazon VPC</strong><span><code>10.0.0.0/16</code></span></div>
  </div>
  <div class="flow-row">
    <div class="flow-box"><strong>🌐 Internet Gateway</strong><span>created &amp; attached automatically</span></div>
    <div class="flow-box"><strong>🔒 Security Group</strong><span>TCP 443 from <code>10.0.0.0/16</code> only</span></div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="az-grid">
  <div class="az-col">
    <h5>Availability Zone 1</h5>
    <div class="sub-box"><strong>Public subnet 1</strong>route → 0.0.0.0/0 via IGW</div>
    <div class="sub-box"><strong>Private-isolated subnet 1</strong>no internet route</div>
  </div>
  <div class="az-col">
    <h5>Availability Zone 2</h5>
    <div class="sub-box"><strong>Public subnet 2</strong>route → 0.0.0.0/0 via IGW</div>

</div>

## Unit testing the CDK code

```bash
uv run pytest tests/unit/test_03_vpc.py -v
```

<div class="columns">
  <div class="col">
    <h4>🧪 What it does</h4>
    <p>Builds the stack with the shared <code>config</code> fixture, synthesizes it in memory with <code>aws_cdk.assertions</code>, and asserts on the CloudFormation template — no AWS credentials, no Docker, no floci needed.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="col dark">
    <h4>✅ What it checks</h4>
    <p>The 7 mandatory tags are present (<code>mandatory_tag_pairs()</code>), plus the module's one or two most important resource facts — a count, a key property.</p>
  </div>
</div>

Full explanation, from zero: [`docs/TESTING.md`](../TESTING.md)

## Known limitations

<div class="cards">
  <div class="card"><div class="icon">🎯</div><h4>floci ≠ AWS exactly</h4><p>Service coverage/fidelity varies by service — see <a href="https://floci.io/aws/">floci — AWS</a> for what's covered.</p></div>
  <div class="card"><div class="icon">🐳</div><h4>Real Docker backends</h4><p>Lambda, RDS, ElastiCache, ECS, EKS, among others, run as actual containers — more faithful, but heavier and slower to start.</p></div>
  <div class="card"><div class="icon">💰</div><h4>Real AWS has real cost</h4><p>NAT Gateway, RDS, OpenSearch, EKS, ElastiCache bill hourly the moment they exist — each README flags this before its optional "Deploy to real AWS" section.</p></div>

<span class="index">05</span>

<span class="kicker">Section 05</span>

# 🧩 Beyond the 44 Modules

Two follow-ups for when a team is ready to go past independent, one-service lessons: combining several services into one SOLID application, and bringing existing resources under CDK.

---

<span class="kicker"><code>examples/enterprise_stack/</code> — a second, different example</span>

## One combined app, 14 resources, SOLID principles

Not a 45th module — a separate CDK app showing how a team combines several of these same services into one cohesive application: enable/disable per environment, real inter-resource dependencies, no giant `if/elif` chain.

<div class="cards cols-3 tight">
  <div class="card"><h4>S — Single Responsibility</h4><p>One <code>*ResourceBuilder</code> class, one AWS resource — 13 files, 13 jobs.</p></div>
  <div class="card"><h4>O — Open/Closed</h4><p>Add resource #14: one new file + one line in <code>builders/__init__.py</code>. Nothing else changes.</p></div>
  <div class="card"><h4>L — Liskov Substitution</h4><p>The stack's loop calls <code>.build()</code> on any builder, interchangeably, with no special-casing.</p></div>
  <div class="card"><h4>I — Interface Segregation</h4><p><code>ResourceContext</code> carries only <code>config</code> + a small <code>shared</code> dict — never 12 resources' worth of unused options.</p></div>
  <div class="card"><h4>D — Dependency Inversion</h4><p><code>LambdaBuilder</code> depends on "an <code>iam_role</code> in context", never on the <code>IamBuilder</code> class itself.</p></div>
</div>

Full explanation, plus a no-code "without SOLID" comparison: [`examples/enterprise_stack/README.md`](../../examples/enterprise_stack/README.md)

---

<span class="kicker">Conditional resources, precedence, and "cells"</span>

## Same code, different environments, accounts, and regions

<div class="flow">
  <div class="flow-row">
    <div class="flow-box dark"><strong>environments/dev.json</strong><span>1 cell · 6 resources · no explicit account</span></div>
    <div class="flow-box dark"><strong>environments/staging.json</strong><span>1 cell · 13 resources (full app, no EC2)</span></div>
    <div class="flow-box accent"><strong>environments/prod.json</strong><span>2 cells · all 14 resources each</span></div>
  </div>
  <div class="flow-arrow down">↓</div>
  <div class="flow-row">
    <div class="flow-box"><strong>cell-01</strong><span><code>us-east-1</code></span></div>
    <div class="flow-box"><strong>cell-02</strong><span><code>us-west-2</code></span></div>
  </div>
</div>

Turning a resource on/off is listing its key in JSON; ordering (e.g. VPC before EC2) is a topological sort over each builder's `depends_on` — enabling a resource without its dependency raises a clear error, it never silently auto-enables anything. Cells reuse this repo's own `cell_based`/`cell_id` tags (`shared/tagging.py`) — the only difference between the two prod cells is 4 lines of JSON.

---

<span class="kicker">A question every team hits once an AWS account isn't brand new</span>

## Importing existing resources into CDK

| Situation | Use |
|---|---|
| Your code just needs to *read* a resource another stack owns | `from_*` (e.g. `Bucket.from_bucket_arn()`) — a read-only proxy, never managed |
| You need to select a complex resource (like a VPC) by tag/default-ness | `Vpc.from_lookup()` — queries the account at synth time |
| A known, existing resource should come under your stack's management | `cdk import` — exact preconditions and workflow documented |
| No CDK app yet — generate one from an account scan, stack, or template | `cdk migrate --from-scan` / `--from-stack` / `--from-path` |

Practice the whole workflow at zero cost against floci before ever trying it against a real account: [`docs/IMPORTING-EXISTING-RESOURCES.md`](../IMPORTING-EXISTING-RESOURCES.md)
